analysis.one_liner: Caps federal student loan payments at 10% of income and forgives remaining balances after ten years of payments.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2012 with 24 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let federal student loan borrowers cap their monthly payments at 10% of income above a poverty-line threshold, and forgive whatever balance remained after 120 monthly payments, counting months of economic-hardship deferment as payments. It would have capped interest on new federal direct loans at 3.4%, let some borrowers with high-interest private loans refinance into federal loans at 3.4%, cut the public-service forgiveness waiting period from 120 to 60 payments, and made forgiven debt tax-free. The bill was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers, especially those with low or moderate incomes and those carrying high-interest private loans: their payments would be limited to 10% of income above roughly 150% of the poverty line, balances would be erased after ten years of qualifying payments, public-service workers would get forgiveness after five years instead of ten, and eligible private loan borrowers could move into federal loans capped at 3.4% interest. Forgiven balances would not count as taxable income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal and private student loan borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a 10/10 repayment plan limiting monthly payments on federal Family Education Loans and Direct Loans to one-twelfth of 10% of income above 150% of the poverty line, with unpaid interest not capitalized and remaining balances forgiven after 120 monthly payments.
Counts months in economic-hardship deferment as payments toward the ten-year forgiveness threshold, protecting borrowers who hit hard times from losing ground.
Caps the interest rate on all new federal direct loans at 3.4%, down from higher statutory rates in effect at the time.

Allows certain borrowers to consolidate existing private education loans into federal Direct Consolidation Loans capped at 3.4% interest during a one-year application window, targeting borrowers whose income is less than their total education debt.
Cuts the public-service loan forgiveness requirement from 120 payments to 60 and adds primary care physicians in medically underserved areas as eligible.
Excludes forgiven loan amounts from gross income, so borrowers would not owe taxes on canceled debt.

analysis.who_pays: The federal budget bears the cost: it pays private loan holders in full when loans are consolidated, absorbs forgiven balances, and forgoes interest above 3.4%. The bill directs these costs to funds available for Overseas Contingency Operations — the war-spending account — rather than raising taxes. Private student loan lenders lose future high-interest revenue on loans bought out under the refinancing provision.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and private loan lenders

drawbacks.text: The price tag is large: the federal government would absorb forgiven balances on up to a trillion dollars of outstanding debt and pay private lenders in full for consolidated loans, and the bill's only offset is a direction to spend from the Overseas Contingency Operations account, which does not actually raise money to cover the cost.

Relief is not unlimited: for people who borrow after enactment, forgiveness is capped at $45,520 in principal and fees plus accrued interest, and under the repayment plan the payment period can stretch beyond ten years, with unpaid interest accruing until forgiveness.

The private-loan refinancing door is narrow: only loans made on or before enactment qualify, borrowers must apply within one year, and only those whose average income over three years is less than their total education debt are eligible.

Participation requires automatic electronic debit from a bank account for all eligible loan payments, and borrowers whose calculated payment is zero but who are not in hardship deferment face case-by-case payment determinations by the Education Secretary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real and targeted: borrowers paying on incomes below their debt would finally see balances disappear, and private-loan borrowers stuck at high rates would get a 3.4% federal option. But the bill is honestly described as expensive, and its funding mechanism — drawing on war-spending funds — is an accounting choice, not a true pay-for. An honest supporter would concede the net federal cost would be substantial; an honest opponent would concede the bill contains anti-abuse limits (income verification, forgiveness caps, a one-year refinancing window) that narrow who gets relief.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then two subcommittees, and no committee ever brought it up for a markup or vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Hansen Clarke introduced the bill on March 8, 2012, with the stated goal of increasing purchasing power, aiding the economic recovery, and restoring fairness in financing higher education.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and, in addition, to the Foreign Affairs and Armed Services Committees.
In late March 2012 it was referred to the Armed Services Subcommittee on Military Personnel and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training.
No further action was ever taken: there was no committee markup, no floor debate, and no vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill had 24 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of its provisions advanced through the committees to which it was assigned.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders kept collecting high interest with fewer consumer protections, and the federal budget avoided the cost of forgiveness and refinancing. Borrowers got nothing: loan balances continued to grow as they had before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private loan lenders and the federal budget

for.name: Rep. Hansen Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of primary jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote.

against.name: Speaker John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Under the Speaker's authority, referred the bill to three committees simultaneously, splitting jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill, so there is no roll-call record; its sponsor and all 24 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would have bought eligible private loans out at full value but ended the lenders' stream of high-interest, low-protection loan payments, and capped the refinanced rate at 3.4%. Lenders' interest in keeping borrowers at higher rates ran against the borrowers the bill aimed to help.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and FFEL lenders
industries.note: Even under the bill's capped payments, lenders holding guaranteed loans would keep receiving federal special-allowance subsidies calculated on the loan principal and unpaid accrued interest, so the federal guarantee-and-subsidy channel stays in place while borrower payments are limited.
The bill would have expanded the federal Direct Loan program's role by pulling private loans into federal consolidation at 3.4%, growing the federal portfolio while reducing what borrowers owe.
